newsitem.title: UK: EMU's latest twist puts shine in Italian bonds.
newsitem.headline: EMU's latest twist puts shine in Italian bonds.

text.p: Italian government bonds hold promise for investors as the saga over European monetary union takes yet another twist with speculation of a softer approach to the entry conditions for the single currency, analysts said on Monday.
British newspapers reported that German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said at a weekend meeting of European finance ministers that he had "never nailed himself to the cross of three percent".
He was referring to the permissible level of a government's budget deficit as a percent of its gross domestic product as set by the Maastricht Treaty.
Waigel, who has always been a strong proponent of a strict application of the entry test, and other German ministers have since denied any weakening of the deficit criteria.
But analysts said that what was important was not what Waigel said but the interpretation of what he meant.

"The market will see any slippage of the three percent criteria as increasing the chances of a broad EMU (economic and monetary union)," said Ifty Islam, European bond strategist at Merrill Lynch in London.

"Politicians are making clear that they want EMU to go ahead and on time, and with the participation of as many countries as possible," said Han de Jong, head of bond research at ABN Amro Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.
Possible signs of a broad-based EMU would bolster Italy, whose first round entry into the single currency has been subject of much debate, and make the high yield on the country's bonds attractive.

Julian Jessop, European economist at Nikko Europe in London, said that while the next turn in market sentiment would be towards the idea of a soft monetary union, a broad monetary union would be unacceptable to the German public.
"It is clear that they are taking two steps forwards and one step back towards a more flexible position," he said.
"That view is no better than neutral for core markets, but the flip side of it is that it is positive for Italy," he said, adding that he would be bullish on Italy across the yield curve.
"The EMU talk is likely to favour the long end of the (Italian) market but you've also got positive expectations about interest rate cuts which will help the short end," he said.
The yield spread between 10-year Italian government bonds and German Bunds -- an indication of a country's relative risk -- had narrowed to 177 basis points by 1515 GMT from 181 at Friday's close.
The gap surged over the 200 basis point mark in mid-March as concerns about a delay in the start of EMU dogged the market.
De Jong said the potential was for the gap to narrow further over the next few months. "If the market gets a bit enthusiastic it could easily go back to the 150 or 140 level," he said.
Islam also said further convergence was likely but would be driven by rising yields in the mark bloc rather than a significant further fall in 10-year yields in Italy and Spain.
"There is an upwards risk to yields globally in the 10-year area," he said. "But on a fundamental view a case can be made at the short end of Italy."

He said two-year yields were currently above money rates and the rebound on the dollar should be accompanied by a further recovery of the lira, which in turn would be supportive of establishing outright long positions at the short end of Italy.
Jessop said the move in EMU sentiment might also be potentially positive for British gilts, which investors could use as a safe haven.
"But I am a little bit wary of piling into the UK when it is only a few weeks before the election."
